description: When a Georgia child is hurt on an e-bike or golf cart, the first question is what exactly the machine was. The answer can decide who pays.
shortAnswer: When a child is hurt on a motorized machine, the first question in the claim is often what exactly was this thing? The answer can decide who pays. A machine with more than 750 watts, or with pedals that are only for show, may not be an electric assisted bicycle at all.

sections.heading: An e-bike is not always an e-bike
sections.shortAnswer: Georgia law defines an “electric assisted bicycle” in O.C.G.A. § 40-1-1. It has two or three wheels, a saddle, fully operative pedals, and a motor of not more than 750 watts.

sections.heading: Golf carts are not a toy under Georgia law
sections.shortAnswer: The state statute says all operators of those vehicles must have a valid driver’s license. There is one exception, for a locality that passed an ordinance before January 1, 2012. You have to read the local ordinance.

sections.heading: If a car hits your child
sections.shortAnswer: Riding a machine illegally does not end the case. The question is still who caused the crash.

sections.heading: If your child is hurt with no car involved
sections.shortAnswer: If a parent hands a dangerous machine to a child who cannot handle it, that parent may be liable for negligent entrustment. Many homeowner’s policies limit or exclude coverage for motorized vehicles. Get the policy before you count on it.

sections.heading: What about the helmet?
sections.shortAnswer: Under O.C.G.A. § 40-6-296(d), a person under 16 may not ride a bicycle on a public road, path, or sidewalk without a helmet. A violation of the bicycle helmet subsection is not negligence per se.

sections.heading: Before you buy one
sections.shortAnswer: Check the watts, the pedals, and the top speed. Find out whether your child can legally ride it where you live. Ask whether your homeowner’s and auto policies cover this machine, and get the answer in writing.

sections.heading: If your child is hurt
sections.shortAnswer: Do not repair, sell, or throw away the machine. It is the evidence. Do not give a recorded statement to any insurance company before you get advice.

faq.q: What counts as an e-bike under Georgia law?
faq.a: Georgia law defines an “electric assisted bicycle” in O.C.G.A. § 40-1-1. It has two or three wheels, a saddle, fully operative pedals, and a motor of not more than 750 watts.

faq.q: Does a child need a driver's license to drive a golf cart on a Georgia street?
faq.a: The state statute says all operators of those vehicles must have a valid driver’s license. There is one exception, for a locality that passed an ordinance before January 1, 2012 allowing use on the streets without a license. You have to read the local ordinance.

faq.q: Will homeowner's insurance cover a child hurt on an e-bike or golf cart?
faq.a: Many homeowner’s policies limit or exclude coverage for motorized vehicles, often with exceptions that depend on where the vehicle was being used. The exact policy wording controls. Get the policy before you count on it, and report the injury promptly.
